newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil govt calls Congress' bluff over re-election.
newsitem.headline: Brazil govt calls Congress' bluff over re-election.

text.p: The Brazilian government's insistence on voting next week a bill on re-election surprised many in Congress, where even allies of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso doubted they had enough votes, newspapers said.

Newspapers reported Friday that many deputies regarded the government's brinkmanship as an attempt to call the bluff of opponents within its ranks, in particular, rebellious members of the powerful Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB).
"If they vote next week, the government will lose. The government's bluffing," PMDB deputy Henrique Eduardo Alves told reporters after a meeting of government leaders late Thursday.

The Folha de Sao Paulo newspaper said the maneuver was intended to pressure opponents into showing their true colours and that in reality, January 29 was a more likely date for the bill to be put to a first vote on the chamber floor.

"If you don't set a deadline, you won't reach a deal. And with a deadline looming, our group (of pro re-election deputies) will stick close together," deputy Jose Jorge of the leadership of the government-allied Liberal Front Party (PFL) told Folha.

Whatever the government's nebulous strategy, observers predicted the Cardoso camp would be negotiating feverishly over the weekend and early next week to muster the 308 votes it needs to pass the constitional amendment.
Cardoso's bid to become Brazil's first re-elected president hit turbulence last weekend when PMDB rebels hijacked a party conference and engineered a vote against re-election.
The government won a significant victory this week in persuading PMDB deputies to help it pass the bill in a special lower house committee.
But PMDB leaders still insist they will not allow a vote on the plenary floor until elections for the Senate and Chamber of Deputies presidencies have been settled in early February.

Lower house PFL leader Inocencio Oliveira's declaration late Thursday that the vote would take place next week contrasted with the general impression that the government knew it had to strike a deal with the PMDB, whose votes are essential.

Senate President Jose Sarney, a PMDB leader who would prefer not to see Cardoso seek a second term but who is widely seen as willing to trade his opposition to re-election for government concessions in other areas, urged Cardoso not to bully Congress.
Sarney said Cardoso's stated aim to "break the PMDB in half" and to use the threat of a plebiscite to pressure Congress into making a rapid decision on re-election could misfire.
"You can't shut up a fiddle by shouting at it," he wrote in a weekly newspaper column, quoting a proverb from the northeast.
